originalGroup.material:
The ferry across the blue mat

Leo puts a blue mat on the floor and calls it a river. His toy cars wait on one side. He uses a wide lid as a ferry, moving it slowly across the mat. His sister makes a paper sign that says Ferry. One red car is too wide for the lid, so Leo leaves it beside the river and carries the smaller cars first. He does not push the red car into the pretend water. Later, he finds a wider tray for a second ferry. The red car can cross on that one. At the end, the cars and trays return to their boxes.

originalGroup.material:
How a zip closes

A zip fastener joins two flexible edges with rows of small teeth. The teeth do not simply sit beside one another: their shapes allow them to ____1____ when brought together by a slider. The result is a continuous fastening that can later be opened again.

The slider has internal channels that guide the two rows into the right ____2____. Moving it in one direction brings the rows together. Moving it the other way separates them. Its shape therefore controls a sequence, rather than holding every tooth itself.

For the mechanism to work, the teeth must be properly ____3____. A damaged or displaced section can interrupt the closing action. Pulling harder does not necessarily solve the problem and may make the damage worse.

The surrounding ____4____ also matters. Fabric caught near the slider can obstruct movement even when the teeth are sound. A user may need to stop and inspect the cause rather than treat every difficulty as a failure of the metal or plastic parts.

Different products make different ____5____ on a fastening. A small clothing zip and a heavy bag zip may share a principle while differing in size, material and construction. The chosen design needs to suit the intended ____6____.

A closed zip can ____7____ force along many joined teeth, but it still has limits. The fastening is not a reason to overfill a bag beyond what the product can handle. Care involves using the whole object ____8____, not only checking whether the slider reaches the end.

The mechanism is familiar partly because its useful action is ____9____: a short hand movement changes a long edge from open to closed. Understanding the parts makes that ordinary movement easier to explain. It also helps distinguish a temporary obstruction from damage that needs proper ____10____.

originalGroup.material:
When a catalogue search returns nothing

An empty catalogue search can seem to offer a definite answer: the collection contains nothing relevant. That conclusion depends, however, on the relation between the search and the catalogue's ____1____. A database of descriptions is not necessarily a complete transcription of every document.

The words used in a query may differ from those used by the cataloguer. A modern place name may have an older ____2____, and a person may appear under initials. A search can therefore fail to ____3____ an item that is present but described differently.

The level of description matters too. A box-level entry may name a broad topic while omitting the names contained in individual letters. The absence of a name from the catalogue is not automatically ____4____ of its absence from the box.

A useful search strategy makes its ____5____ explicit. It records which catalogue, terms and filters were used. Without that information, another researcher cannot distinguish a careful unsuccessful search from a brief attempt with a narrow query.

This does not require treating every negative result as worthless. It requires a ____6____ account of what the result can support. Searching a well-defined, fully transcribed list may justify a stronger conclusion than searching a selective description of mixed papers.

Researchers can ____7____ their approach by trying variant names, broader categories or advice from collection staff. Each step should answer a particular limitation rather than expand the search indefinitely without purpose.

The final report can state that no matching entry was found under the specified conditions. That wording preserves the result without ____8____ it into a claim about every possible source. It also keeps the work ____9____ to later checking. A negative search becomes more informative when its boundaries are part of the ____10____ rather than hidden behind the word nothing.

A sponge can be useful for spreading or removing liquid, but its ____5____ must be considered. Picking up water does not mean it destroys dirt or makes an unclean surface safe by itself. Cleaning involves more than the physical movement of liquid.

After use, retained water may remain in the ____6____. The way a sponge is cleaned, dried and replaced should follow suitable guidance for its task. The same object should not be moved carelessly between uses with different hygiene requirements.

A user may judge the sponge by how ____7____ it feels, but a full explanation involves internal structure and material behaviour. The familiar action of squeezing links a hand movement to a change inside an object we cannot see through.

Simple comparisons can help ____8____ that link. Observing water entering and leaving makes the process more concrete, even without measuring every pore. Such a demonstration should be described ____9____, with conclusions limited to what was actually compared. A useful everyday explanation connects an observable result with a plausible ____10____ while keeping the practical limits in view.

A translator's footnote can make a difficult choice visible, but the presence of a note does not automatically make the choice ____1____. Readers still need to know what problem the note addresses and how it relates to the surrounding passage.

Some words have a range of associations that no single substitute can ____2____. A note may identify a cultural reference, explain a pun or describe an alternative reading. These are different functions, and combining them without distinction can obscure the translator's ____3____.

A useful note has an appropriate ____4____. Too little information may leave the difficulty untouched, while an extensive essay can interrupt a passage whose force depends on movement. The decision involves the work's purpose and likely readers, not a universal ideal number of words.

originalGroup.material:
A route through a museum

A museum route (0) IS a choice about sequence as well as space. Visitors may feel that they are simply walking through a building, ____1____ each doorway places one encounter before another. That order can shape the account they take away.

There is no point ____2____ pretending a route can include everything equally. Some objects receive a central position, while others remain at the edge. The useful question is not whether selection occurs, ____3____ how it is made and explained.

A route may move from early to late events, or from one theme to another. Neither arrangement speaks ____4____ itself. Labels and transitions help visitors understand what kind of connection they are being invited to make.

The account can be clear without claiming that every object has only one meaning. As ____5____ as practical access is considered, alternative paths may offer another way into the material. Visitors need not follow precisely the same sequence to find a thoughtful encounter.

The route should also leave room for someone ____6____ wants to pause, return or skip a section. Designing for an imagined average pace can overlook how differently people use a museum. To some ____7____, a successful route supports choices rather than merely directing feet. It helps visitors make sense of what they meet, while keeping them aware ____8____ the larger collection beyond the chosen path.
